# Reading errors

Red text just appeared. Is the problem in your code, in the notebook your code
is running on, or in your internet? Three different problems, three different
fixes, and picking the wrong one costs you the rest of the evening. The red
text on your screen already says which one you have.

## How much red is normal

There's one way Python tells you it stopped, and it uses that way for a missing
bracket and for a corrupted genome file alike. The amount of red on your screen
says nothing about how badly the work is going. You get back the first thing
the machine couldn't do, and nothing else.

Al Sweigart puts a box in the first chapter of *Automate the Boring Stuff with
Python*, headed ERRORS ARE OKAY. The line inside it is that professional
software developers get error messages all the time while writing code.
Experience buys less time per error, and that time goes on reading rather than
typing.

## Read the last line first

Here's a script called `gc_report.py` that looks fine. It reports GC content
for sequences it looks up by name.

``` {.python}
def gc_fraction(records, name):
    sequence = records[name]
    g_and_c = sequence.count("G") + sequence.count("C")
    return g_and_c / len(sequence)


def report(records, names):
    for name in names:
        print(name, round(gc_fraction(records, name), 4))


records = {"BRCA1_human": "ATGGATTTATCTGCTCTTCGCGTTGAAGAAGTACAAAAT"}
report(records, ["BRCA1_human", "Brca1_mouse"])
```

Those 39 bases are real. They open the *BRCA1* coding sequence, and they come
from the accession you recorded in Chapter 5, `NM_007294.4`. Base 114 of that
transcript is where the coding sequence starts. Run the script and one line of
output arrives before the red does.

``` {.default .output}
BRCA1_human 0.359
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "gc_report.py", line 13, in <module>
    report(records, ["BRCA1_human", "Brca1_mouse"])
  File "gc_report.py", line 9, in report
    print(name, round(gc_fraction(records, name), 4))
  File "gc_report.py", line 2, in gc_fraction
    sequence = records[name]
KeyError: 'Brca1_mouse'
```

Three rows are missing from that block, one under each code line. Your own
screen carries a run of tildes and carets there, pointing at the piece of the
line Python was working on when it stopped. Under line 2 it sits below
`records[name]`, which narrows a long line to the single operation that failed.
They're left off the page here so the frames stay easy to count.

[A Colab line number counts from the top of the cell it's in, not from the top of the notebook.]{.margin}

Colab dresses the same block differently. Chapter 4 showed the shape: a rule of
dashes, a line naming a file Colab built out of your cell, and an arrow
pointing at the code. The frames are the same frames in the same order, and
everything below applies to both.

That block is called a [traceback]{.term def="The block Python prints when it
stops. A list of the lines it was inside, innermost last, then the error."},
and it's printed in the order the machine ran things. You want to read it in
the opposite order. I read tracebacks top down for about a year, and I
abandoned plenty of them before reaching the one sentence written for a person.

Four steps, in this order.

1. Read the last line. It carries a class name, `KeyError`, then a message
   about this failure, `'Brca1_mouse'`.
2. Read the frame directly above it. That's the line Python was on when it
   stopped: `sequence = records[name]`, on line 2.
3. Ask whether that line could be right and still fail. Here it can. Looking a
   name up in a dictionary is correct; the name it got was wrong.
4. Walk up one frame at a time until you reach a line you typed today. Line 9
   passed the name along, and line 13 is where you wrote it.

The mistake is on line 13 and the traceback stopped on line 2. The gap is the
normal case. A traceback tells you where the machine gave up, which is
downstream of wherever you were careless.

::: {.check}
Answer three questions off that traceback alone. Which class stopped it? Which
key was missing? Which line was running at the moment it stopped? The answers
are `KeyError`, `'Brca1_mouse'`, and line 2. If you answered line 13 for the
third, you read the frames in call order instead of from the bottom.
:::

## Which of the four voices is this

Chapter 4 named four things that can interrupt you, one more than the question
this chapter opened on. The fourth is a website, and it only interrupts you
while you're filling in a form. Now you can tell all four apart by what they
print.

Python is talking when there's a class name in the message and a line of your
own code above it. The eight classes below are all Python.

The notebook runtime is talking when there's no class name and no line of your
code anywhere. The line `Your session crashed after using all available RAM.`
is about the machine, and your code goes unmentioned because your code isn't
what failed.

A website is talking when your form is still on the screen and a colored strip
has appeared next to one of the boxes you filled in. There's no line number,
because you never wrote a line.

The network is talking when nothing happens at all. No message, no output, and
a ring that keeps turning. That's the one voice you diagnose by waiting.

## The eight errors, most expensive first

These are ordered by what they cost you, not by how often you'll meet them. A
`NameError` is the one you'll see most and the one you'll fix fastest. A
`KeyError` on a gene identifier is rare and can take your whole evening, so it
goes first. Every message below came out of a real interpreter, Python 3.14.5,
on 2 August 2026. Older Pythons say less inside these messages. The class name
at the front is the part that hasn't moved.

### KeyError

``` {.default .output}
KeyError: 'BRCA1'
```

A `KeyError` names the key you asked for and gives you nothing else. The name
is the whole message. The dictionary holds no entry filed under `'BRCA1'`, so
the lookup stopped there.

What makes it expensive is what the missing key usually turns out to be. In
real work it's a gene identifier. Your counts table is keyed on `Brca1` and
your gene list says `BRCA1`, and Chapter 3 already warned you that two
nomenclature committees enforce that difference on purpose. So a `KeyError` on
an identifier means your two inputs disagree about what things are called.

::: {.why}
The disagreement is itself a finding. Gene symbols get renamed, and they get
reused across species with different capitalization. When two genes turn out to
be one, they get merged under a single symbol, and the retired one stops
matching anything. A failed lookup is the machine telling you that two files
describe the same biology under two naming schemes. Chapter 20 hands you 27,179
rows keyed on Entrez IDs for exactly this reason.
:::

Fix it by looking at the keys rather than at the code. Put a few real keys next
to the one you asked for with `print(sorted(records)[:6], name)`, and the
difference is usually visible on sight. There's a second fix that looks tidier
and is worse.

::: {.trap}
`records.get(name, 0)` returns a default instead of stopping. Reach for it here
and every mismatched gene now reads zero. The table fills up, every plot
renders, and nothing says that half your genes were never found. Use a default
only where a missing key is expected and means something. Otherwise you've
traded a loud failure for a quiet wrong answer.
:::

### FileNotFoundError

``` {.default .output}
FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: 'counts.tsv'
```

`[Errno 2]` is the operating system's own number for this, passed straight
through. Some line of your code asked for a file by that name, in the folder
the notebook is working in, and there isn't one there.

The trouble is that the folder isn't on your computer. The notebook runs on a
machine at Google, so a file in your own Downloads folder is invisible to it no
matter how clearly you can see it. And a file you upload into a session goes
away when the runtime restarts, along with every variable.

Ask the runtime what it can actually reach before you open anything:

``` {.python}
import os
print("counts.tsv" in os.listdir())
```

``` {.default .output}
False
```

Print `sorted(os.listdir())` on its own line to see every name instead of one.
Every file this book uses arrives by a line of code inside the notebook, so
when the name you want isn't there, run that line again.

The name in the quotes is yours, so it moves. In Chapter 20 the same message
ends `'data/GSE60450_counts.tsv.gz'` and means exactly this.

### TypeError

``` {.default .output}
TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str
```

A `TypeError` means the operation exists and the values you handed it are the
wrong kind of thing. That first message is readable: you tried to glue a number
onto the end of some text, and `+` won't do that. Wrap the number in `str()`,
or hand both to `print` separated by a comma.

Now the one that costs you.

``` {.default .output}
TypeError: not all arguments converted during string formatting
```

Nobody was formatting a string. That message turns up when you divide, and
here's why. Between two numbers, `%` gives the remainder. With text on the
left, `%` is old-style string formatting, a separate feature that spells itself
with the same character. So `"39" % 3` isn't Python refusing to divide: it was
formatting the text `"39"`, finding no slot to put the 3 into, and saying so in
the only vocabulary it had.

Anything read from a file, a form or a web page arrives as text. Convert it
with `int()` at the moment it arrives and this error stops being possible.

### IndexError

``` {.default .output}
IndexError: list index out of range
```

Positions start at 0. A list of 13 codons has positions 0 through 12, and there
is no position 13. So `codons[len(codons)]` always asks for one item past the
end, because the length is always one more than the last position. The string
version says `string index out of range` and means the same thing.

Take the last item with `codons[-1]`. Negative positions count back from the
end, and that expression stays correct when the list changes length. The model
behind all this is in Chapter 11, and the error is what it feels like when the
model slips.

### ModuleNotFoundError

``` {.default .output}
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'Bio'
```

The library called `Bio` isn't on that machine. Python looked in every folder
it keeps libraries in and found nothing. This one is on the list for what it
does to people rather than for what it costs to fix. It's the error that ends
courses, usually on the first evening, before any biology has happened.

In this book it has one cause. Chapter 17 opens with `!pip install biopython`,
and Colab throws that installation away whenever the session restarts, so you
run the cell again. Nothing gets installed on your own machine, then or ever.

### IndentationError

``` {.default .output}
IndentationError: expected an indented block after 'for' statement on line 1
```

The left margin is how Python works out what sits inside what. A line ending in
a colon promises a block underneath it, shifted right. When nothing is shifted
right, Python reports that the promised block never arrived and names the line
that made the promise.

Two other wordings come from the same place. The message `unexpected indent`
means you pushed a line right when nothing was expecting a block. The message
`unindent does not match any outer indentation level` means you came back left
to a margin no enclosing block uses.

This one feels arbitrary because the cause is invisible. A tab and four spaces
look identical on screen and are different characters to Python. The usual
cause is a block with both in it, and that mix almost always arrives with text
you pasted in from somewhere else.

### SyntaxError

``` {.default .output}
SyntaxError: '(' was never closed
```

A `SyntaxError` means Python couldn't finish reading your instruction, so it
never ran any of that cell. None of it, including the lines above the one it
points at. Your earlier cells already ran and their variables are still there,
which is why the notebook can look half alive.

The line number is the trap. It marks the point where Python gave up, and for
an unclosed bracket that point is where the bracket was opened. You'll be
staring at a line three below it wondering what's wrong with it.

Recent Pythons name the fix in the message. `expected ':'` means a colon is
missing at the end of a `for` or `if` line. The message
`invalid syntax. Maybe you meant '==' or ':=' instead of '='?` tells you that
you wrote one equals sign where a comparison needed two. A quotation mark
copied out of a document can also arrive curly, and the message then names that
character and prints its Unicode number.

### NameError

``` {.default .output}
NameError: name 'sequnce' is not defined. Did you mean: 'sequences'?
```

Python reached a name it had never been given a value for. Read the whole line
before you look at your code. The second sentence is Python comparing your name
against every name it knows, then handing you the closest match. It's right
often enough to try first.

Two causes sit behind it. One is a typo, which the suggestion catches. The
other is that the cell defining the name is sitting above this one, unrun, and
no suggestion can catch that: the name genuinely doesn't exist yet. Restart and
run all sorts it out.

The second sentence arrived in Python 3.10. Run the same code on 3.9 and the
last line stops after `is not defined`, with nothing after it. Some notebook
front ends drop it too, which Python's own release notes warn about. The class
and the name are the message, and the suggestion is a convenience on top.

## Finding a wrong answer by halving

Some code runs cleanly and hands you a number that's wrong. Here are six lines
that do that. They pull the sequence out of a FASTA record and report GC
content.

``` {.python}
raw = ">NM_007294.4\nATGGATTTATCTGCT\nCTTCGCGTTGAAGAA\nGTACAAAAT"
lines = raw.split("\n")
sequence = "".join(lines)
g_and_c = sequence.count("G") + sequence.count("C")
gc_fraction = g_and_c / len(sequence)
print("GC content:", round(gc_fraction, 4))
```

``` {.default .output}
GC content: 0.2745
```

No red anywhere. The answer is wrong, and the only reason you know is that the
true value for those 39 bases is 0.359 and you could count them by hand.

The instinct is to put a `print` after every line. Resist it. Six lines gives
you six prints to read and sixty lines gives you sixty, and reading them is the
same work as reading the code. Cut the suspect region in half instead.

The script is six lines, so put one `print` at the halfway mark, just after
line 3 runs. Print a length rather than a sequence, because a length you can
check against a number you already know.

``` {.python}
print(len(sequence))
```

``` {.default .output}
51
```

You expected 39. So the fault is in lines 1 to 3 and lines 4 to 6 are innocent.
Halve what's left again: put a `print` after line 2 instead.

``` {.python}
print(len(lines))
```

``` {.default .output}
4
```

That one's correct. A header line and three sequence lines is exactly four. The
fault has to be line 3. Look straight at it: `"".join(lines)` glues the header
onto the front of the sequence. Use `lines[1:]` instead and the denominator
drops from 51 to 39.

Two prints found it. Each one halved what was left, so a script of about sixty
lines takes six, because doubling one six times gets you past sixty. Printing
after every line takes sixty.

::: {.check}
Run the fixed version and you should get `GC content: 0.359`. If you get
`0.2745` again, you edited one cell and re-ran a different one.
:::

::: {.trap}
A cell that fails halfway through still did everything above the line that
failed. Those variables keep their new values while the ones below keep their
old ones, and nothing on screen marks which is which. Run a later cell now and
the number it prints is arithmetic on a mixture of two runs. After any error,
restart and run all before you trust anything.
:::

## Cutting an error message down to what's searchable

An error message has two parts and only one of them is worth putting in a
search box. The machine's part is the class name and the fixed wording. Your
part is everything Python quoted back at you: your filenames, your variable
names, your keys.

Search `NameError: name 'sequnce' is not defined` whole and you're searching
for your own typo. Drop the quoted name, search
`NameError name is not defined python`, and you get the class.

Same move on the file error. Cut `'counts.tsv'` and keep
`FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory`. Then add one word for
where it ran, which for everything in this book is `colab`.

One exception, and it matters. When the quoted part is somebody else's name
rather than yours, keep it. The whole line `No module named 'Bio'` is worth
searching, because `Bio` isn't a name you invented.

## Asking a question somebody will answer

A question gets answered when a stranger can reproduce your problem in under a
minute without asking you anything first. That's the whole standard, and it's
the one part of the transaction you control.

Take script 5 from the exercise below. It's seventeen lines. Cut everything
that isn't needed to still get the same error: the loop, the list
comprehension, and seven of the eight codons in the table.

``` {.python}
codon_table = {"ATG": "M"}
print(codon_table["CTT"])
```

``` {.default .output}
KeyError: 'CTT'
```

Two lines, and anybody can paste them and get the same last line you got. What
you've built is a [minimal reproducible example]{.term def="The smallest code
that still produces your error, with everything unrelated removed."}. Do the
cutting before you write the question. Every line you delete is a line you've
ruled out, which is the same work as finding the bug, and it sometimes finishes
the job before you post anything.

Then post five things, in this order.

1. What you were trying to get, in one sentence, in biology terms.
2. The cut-down code, as text you can select. Never a screenshot.
3. The error, complete and verbatim, from the first line to the last.
4. The things you already tried, and what happened when you tried them.
5. Where it ran. "Google Colab" is enough.

Screenshots are the common mistake. Nobody can search a picture, and the person
reading your question wants to paste your message into the same box you did.

Biostars takes questions with biology in them and Stack Overflow takes ones
that are purely about Python. Both are public archives, so a well-formed
question keeps working for the next person who hits the same wall. Those
archives are the whole substitute for having somebody two doors down.

## Exercises

Predict before you run, on all five. Work through each script, write down the
class you expect, then run it. A wrong prediction is worth more than a right
one here, because it points at the exact thing you believed that isn't true.

::: {.exercise num="16.1" time="60 minutes"}
::: {.goal}
Diagnose and fix five broken scripts, committing to the error class in writing
before you change anything.
:::
::: {.given}
`scripts/broken/broken_1.py` through `broken_5.py`, in the repository Chapter 3
names. Copy the text of one script into a Colab cell and run it. Each script
breaks in exactly one way and no two break the same way. Worked answers are in
`scripts/solutions/`, one per script, and each says what the machine believed
as well as what to change.
:::
::: {.produce}
Five error class names, in script order, each written down before you fix
anything. Then five working scripts, each producing the output its comment
header describes.
:::
::: {.check}
All five class names you wrote down are different. If two of them match, one is
wrong, so go back to the last line of that message. Here are two more checks on
individual scripts. Script 1 has two places the missing bracket could go and
only one of them is right, so read your answer: a GC content of 8.1538 is not a
fraction of anything. Script 3 complains about string formatting while you were
trying to divide, which is the intended surprise; the `TypeError` section
explains what `%` did.
:::

::: {.answerspace lines="10"}
:::
:::

## If it breaks

::: {.ifbreaks}
::: {.errfix err="IndentationError: unexpected indent"}
Python is speaking, and the first line of what you pasted arrived with spaces
in front of it. Copying out of a PDF picks up the page's left margin. Put your
cursor at the start of that line and delete backwards until it's flush.
:::

::: {.errfix err="FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: 'broken_1.py'"}
This one is Python speaking, and it's right: the script is in the repository,
not on the machine your notebook is running on. Copy the text of the script
into a cell and run the cell.
:::

::: {.errfix err="The last line ends at 'is not defined' with no suggestion after it"}
Nothing is wrong here. That's still Python speaking, and the suggestion is a
separate feature that arrived in Python 3.10. Some notebook front ends don't
print it even on newer versions. The class and the name are the whole message,
so find the typo by eye: hold the quoted name against the line that made the
variable.
:::

::: {.errfix err="Nothing prints at all and the ring beside the cell keeps turning"}
The runtime is speaking, by saying nothing. None of these five scripts touches
the internet, so nothing in them can wait on a connection. A fresh session
takes a moment to start. Past a minute, restart and run all.
:::
:::

::: {.checkpoint}
- Read a traceback from the bottom up, and name the class, the message, and the
  line that was running when it stopped
- Say which of the four voices produced a message you're looking at
- Name what the machine believed for each of the eight errors in this chapter
- Locate a wrong answer by halving the code under suspicion instead of printing
  every line
- Cut an error message down to the part worth searching, and say which part you
  dropped
- Build a two-line reproducible example out of a script that fails
:::
